title: DEEP DIVE — Everything Looks at Everything
blurb: 2014–2018. The Transformer, built one part at a time. For twenty years language had to be read in order; then attention, and a lunch-table idea that colleagues doubted. Fire the slow reader, keep the attention: three cards per word, one jug of light, a division by eight, eight heads, a clock face for position, talk then think six times. The title, why it won and what it costs, a twenty-year candle put out, and the writing half of the machine, with its curtain over the words to come.

shots.setting: a long, high hall of hanging paper word-slips at dusk, out of time (the inside of a recurrent network); the candle shelf at its foot
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a long hall of hanging word-slips where a scribe carries one lamp from slip to slip in order, and the light he carries fades to a glow-worm at the far end. CHAPTER INDEX TAB (the film's chapter-card device for clue chapters): at the shot's first frame a manila index tab, typed in Special Elite with the chapter title 'DEEP DIVE · Everything Looks at Everything', drops down from the frame's top edge at top-left, like a file-divider tab on a manila folder, holds for 2.5 seconds over the picture, and slides back up; no new shot, no lamp change. CAMERA: the long hall (era location), with one SHELF ledge slid into its foreground (low macro on the read-in-order candle). From black, a single lamp, under the tab. Silently, in the lead-in (no line names it), a ghost of chapter 8's pierced stencil hangs in the haze above the hall and thins away into it (convolution is not in the Transformer; only its lesson, learn the features, carries on), before the scribe sets off. We are at one end of a very long hall: a line of paper word-slips hangs from a beam, receding into haze, dozens of them. A small cut-paper scribe (no real person) walks the line with one lamp, stopping at every slip in turn: he reads it, then passes the lamp's flame forward to a wick on the next slip, step by step, on twos. The camera tracks with him slowly, then pulls back to show how long the line is. This is chapter 6's whisper made visible: the light he carries dims a little at each hand-off, so by the far end it is a glow-worm (the vanishing signal; at about slip 50 it is nearly gone). On 'candle' a short ledge of the candle shelf slides into the hall's foreground and its candle is picked out, standing in its year's place on the shelf (CANDLE PLACEMENT: by the year on the base tag, so left of the 1999 and 2006 candles) (STUDY LOCK: the candle's own flame throws a small candleAmber pool, a practical inside the duskRose hall; the study shelf proper is seen in candleAmber in ch10-s13b): LANGUAGE MUST BE READ IN ORDER (lettered on the candle itself in small caps; base tag 1997). CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Here the candle is still lit: a ghost sleeve about seventeen rings tall (102 px) stands above the stub, the flame where sleeve meets stub; it will go out at twenty rings in ch10-s13b. At its foot, small, the chapter 6 'protected pipe' (the long-memory unit) glows on 'pipe', the callback the line makes: the date the candle was lit, and the reason the belief held so long. In the short music-only hold after L1002 the glow-worm light crawls on down the long dim line (Polosukhin's 'a thousand cycles' quote moves to the end-credits sources card).

shots.setting: a parchment plate in a translator's study, 2014: English word-slips across the top, French down the side
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a whole sentence folded into one envelope jams in a funnel; then the plate opens into a grid where each French word looks back at every English word. Cut (same mood, same sequence) to a parchment plate. First, the old way, as the narration names it. A whole English sentence is folded, slip by slip, into one small sealed envelope (the single list of numbers), and the envelope is squeezed through a narrow paper funnel before a French sentence is written out on the far side. As the sentence is squeezed into the funnel the Bahdanau quote card sets in beside it and stays up through the line, read under the narration (the narration names the bottleneck as the envelope jams; the card shows whose word it was). Then the plate opens into a grid: English slips along the top ('the agreement on the European Economic Area'), French slips down the side ('l'accord sur la zone économique européenne'), the words lettered on the slips themselves (no overlay). As each French word is written, a highlighter of light sweeps across the English row and squares light by how much the translator looks back at each word. The lit squares march along the diagonal and then BEND where French reverses the order (European Economic Area → zone économique européenne), forming the classic alignment heat-map. Every visual square is bound to an attention weight; the map is redrawn from the paper's figure, not copied.

lines.text: In 2014, translating machines squeezed a whole sentence into one list of numbers: a bottleneck. So they learned to look back at every word: attention.

shots.setting: Google, 2016: a Google cafe table at lunch; a warmer dinner-table pool at the rim
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: lunch at Google, 2016: the ghost scribe is lifted away from the table as Uszkoreit suggests keeping only the attention, and a colleague at the rim shrugs. Cut to a sunny-dusk cafe: a long table, trays, two figures in silhouette across from each other. A tall man (Uszkoreit) sketches with a fork in the air; across the table, Polosukhin. On 'only' a ghost of the scribe from shot 1 appears above the table and is lifted away by a paper hand: keep the attention, drop the slow reader. Then the Edge of the Light: a small new lamp stands on the table and its pool spreads. In the breath before L1007 a colleague (Kelcey) steps into the rim, in shadow and facing out; on 'doubted' he gives a brief shrug. As he steps in, Kelcey's quote card rises beside him and stays up through the line and the music-only hold after L1007, so it can be read; in the hold nothing else moves but the haze and the lamp. Two images that teach one thing: a new light, and doubt at its rim.

shots.setting: the hall of word-slips from shot 1, 2017: the scribe is gone
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the scribe sets down his lamp and leaves; every slip lights at once with threads between every pair, and the banner inks The Transformer. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots, see staging.kitWork): threadsOfLight must accept a {tokens, weights[h][i][j]} override (it is hard-wired to the kit's sample sentence). Crossfade back to the long hall with a tint crossfade (crossfadeMood duskRose to serverCyan, no dip to black; the line waits until the cyan is fully up). On 'Drop' the scribe sets his lamp down and simply walks out of frame. On 'attention' the slips hang dark for a held beat, the abandoned lamp's small pool the only light. Then, on 'once', every slip lights at the same instant and threads of light shoot between every pair of slips at once (threadsOfLight, all queries, low opacity), so the hall fills with a fine web of light in a single step instead of a slow procession. The camera, which tracked slowly in shot 1, now holds still: nothing needs to travel. On 'Transformer' its name, THE TRANSFORMER, inks itself onto a parchment banner (prop lettering) hung from the beam (the abstract's phrase moves to the end-credits sources card); on 'title' (L1024) the paper's title inks itself beneath it on the same banner, ATTENTION IS ALL YOU NEED, prop lettering in the banner's own hand; and with it, a third, smaller line in the same hand lists all eight authors in the paper's own order (its footnote says the order is random, and all contributed equally): Vaswani · Shazeer · Parmar · Uszkoreit · Jones · Gomez · Kaiser · Polosukhin (the 2017 date stamp sits beside it), so no one leaves thinking it was a two-person lunch idea (the deadline night, the title's coining and the random author order are in the published sources list), and the web glows through a short hold.

shots.setting: close on three word-slips in the hall, 2017
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: one word-slip turns into numbers and grows three cards, a lantern (question), a mirror (label) and a sealed note (message), each on a knob the messenger tunes. Close on one hanging word-slip. On 'numbers' the slip's lettering briefly dissolves into a short column of small inked numerals (a word is a list of numbers to the machine), then settles back. As each card is named, the slip grows it: on 'question' a small paper lantern with a beam (the query: it shines outward, looking for something); on 'label' a small hand mirror with a tag (the key: what this word offers to be found by); on 'message' a sealed paper note (the value: what it hands over if chosen). On 'tuned' three small brass knobs (the film's 1958 knob, the adjustable weight) appear between the slip and its three objects, one knob per card, each turned to its own setting; just after the line, wordless, the dark messenger bead from chapter 5, in its ring of light, runs once along the three knobs and each turns a hair: the cards are made from the word by learned weights, tuned by back-propagation. Then pull back: every slip in the row now carries all three, lantern, mirror and note, the same three objects in every word, and one caption builds up beneath them as each card is named. The objects are drawn the same everywhere from here on, so a viewer can follow them through the next three shots.

lines.text: Each word arrives as a learned list of numbers and grows three cards: a question, what am I looking for? A label, what have I got? A message, what I pass on. All tuned by our messenger.
lines.direction: the teacher's favourite bit; the first sentence plain and grounding, then three clear steps, warm on 'what I pass on'; the last sentence lighter: these cards are learned, not written

shots.setting: a parchment plate hung from the beam in the hall: four word-slips and four lantern-glass cups
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the worked example: bank shines its question on four mirrors, scores 2, 0, 4, 2 are halved, one jug of light pours into four cups, and bank tints to the water's edge. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots, see staging.kitWork): threadsOfLight and attentionMath need {tokens: crossed · the · river · bank, weights, cups: 4, etched shares} overrides; the kit's toy heads are wired to a different sentence. Cut (same mood, same sequence) to a parchment plate hung from the beam in the hall, a small ILLUSTRATIVE tag in its corner. Four word-slips in a row: crossed · the · river · bank. 'bank' raises its small lantern (its question) and the beam touches each slip's mirror (label) in turn. On 'multiply' the gesture of the chapter 8 stencil returns: bank's four question numbers line up against the label's four, each pair multiplies (small ink products), and on 'add' they sum into one score (the dot product, the same multiply-and-add as the stencil). As each match is scored, the score inks beside its slip: 2, 0, 4, 2. On 'halve' a pen strikes through each score and writes the halves beneath: 1, 0, 2, 1. Then a jug of light tips over the row and pours into four lantern-glass cups beneath the slips; the levels are the real softmax of those halved scores, so the cups fill to 20, 7, 53 and 20 in a hundred, each share etched on its own cup's glass (0.20 · 0.07 · 0.53 · 0.20), the river cup clearly fullest. On 'messages' each word's sealed note (its message) is poured out of its cup into 'bank' in those same proportions, river's note by far the largest stream; on 'water's' bank's slip tints from gold to water-blue, and a small meter drawn on the plate settles at water 0.53 · action 0.20 · money 0.20. The numbers are computed (scaled dot product over toy four-number cards), not hand-drawn; the bible's worked example.

shots.setting: the hall of word-slips, 2017: the announcement's example sentence hung across the beam
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the full-size echo of the toy on the hall's banner sentence: bank's threads reach every slip, then the light splits into coloured heads, each with its own pattern. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots, see staging.kitWork): threadsOfLight needs {tokens: the nine-word sentence, weights[h][i][j] hand-set, cups: 9} overrides. Cut back to the wide hall (same mood). The banner of slips now reads the example sentence from Google's 2017 announcement of the Transformer, lettered on the slips: I · arrived · at · the · bank · after · crossing · the · river. A small ILLUSTRATIVE tag hangs at the banner's end. At the shot's first beat the banner settles (the line no longer speaks the look; the picture carries it); on 'real' the slip 'bank' lifts its lantern and threads of light draw out from 'bank' to every other slip (threadsOfLight, query = 'bank', with HAND-SET weights for this sentence; the kit's attentionMath toy heads are built for a different sentence and are NOT used here), and the jug pours into cups beneath the slips; on 'Transformer' the cup under 'river' fills highest, far above the rest. HAND-SET WEIGHTS for 'bank' (one row, sums to 1): I 0.03 · arrived 0.06 · at 0.04 · the 0.04 · bank 0.08 · after 0.03 · crossing 0.10 · the 0.04 · river 0.58. These show what the announcement says a trained model can learn (it 'can learn to immediately attend to the word river'); they are not a trained model's output, and the tag says so. Then, on 'Eight', the camera pulls back and the single colour of light splits: threads in four distinct low-chroma hues fan out from 'bank' at once, each a different head with a different question, drawn from a small HAND-BUILT HEAD TABLE (also ILLUSTRATIVE, four of the eight shown; each row sums to 1 over the nine slips, the named slips taking the share given and the rest spread evenly): head 1 'what am I?' → river 0.58 (the row above); head 2 'what came just before?' → the (4th slip) 0.70; head 3 'what was done?' → arrived 0.45, crossing 0.35; head 4 'who did it?' → I 0.65. One caption: the real model had eight heads of sixty-four numbers each. Hold on the many-coloured web; then, on 'question', every other word lifts its lantern too and the hall glows: every word doing this, all at once. This shot echoes, at full size, the toy plate of ch10-s06 (same three cards, same jug, same cups).

shots.setting: close on the word-slips, each wearing a small paper-cut clock face
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the slips are shuffled and the threads look the same; rehung, each wears a small clock face set by its place in line. The banner's slips are suddenly shuffled into a heap, and the threads look exactly the same: attention alone cannot tell order (a bag of words). The slips rehang in order, and on 'clock' each one is given a small paper-cut clock face pinned at its top corner: a fast hand, a slower hand and a very slow hand. On 'place' the camera tracks along the row: from slip to slip the fast hand jumps a long way, the slower hand a little, the slowest barely moves, so every position's clock face reads differently. Faintly, behind each clock, its hands' angles are traced as a thin strip of waves (sines and cosines, fast to slow): the same thing, said the way the paper says it. The one label sets in with the clocks on 'clock' so it can be read through the track. One image throughout: the clock face. shots.setting: a long loom of light inside the hall, six blocks set left to right
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a long loom of six blocks: in each, threads pass between the words, then each word brightens alone, and the light front travels through all six. KIT DEPENDENCY (blocking for film-shots, see staging.kitWork): transformerLoom needs {causal:false} and horizontal layout. Cut (same mood, same sequence): each word-slip now spools out a ribbon of light (its residual stream) running left to right through a great loom laid out horizontally, transformerLoom with causal: false (this is the 2017 reading half, the encoder, so its threads reach both ways, forward and back). The loom has six blocks in a row. In each block an attention loom passes threads BETWEEN the ribbons (the words talking; thread alpha = the kit's recorded forward pass), then each ribbon passes through its own small paper lantern (the feed-forward step, thinking alone; glow = its activation), and both write back into the ribbon. The camera trucks slowly left to right along the loom as the light front travels (flow), the focus stepping through blocks 0 to 5, six in all, while the original ribbon runs straight through every block like a highway lane (visual only: no line names it). In the music-only hold after L1021 the lane is picked out in light and the short honesty caption is read in silence: untrained toy weights: real bindings.

shots.setting: a rack of eight chips on a parchment plate; a sundial; the hall of slips again
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: why it won: the web collapses into one grid lit on eight graphics chips at once; the catch: doubling the sentence thickens the threads into a wall. Paper wipe: the loom's last frame (ch10-s10) slides off and becomes the parchment plate (same mood, no tint change). The plate: one machine drawn as a single rack with eight slabs. On 'multiplication' the whole web of threads from the hall collapses into a single great grid (a matrix) and all eight slabs light at once, in parallel: no queue, no scribe. On 'chips' the slabs read as what they are, eight graphics chips in one rack, each glowing with its share of the grid (the one sum such chips do best; Aidan Gomez's line on this is in the end-credits sources). Then, wordless in the pause after L1025 (L1024 has already said it won in half a day; the picture shows how), a paper sundial's shadow sweeps half a day; then two piles of coal-like compute blocks stand beside it, the old system's (Google's previous translator, GNMT+RL) tall, the new one about a seventh as high. Then a small ledger drawn on the plate inks its entry in-world: EN→DE 27.3 · 28.4 BLEU. Then THE CATCH: back in the hall, the sentence grows, slip by slip, from ten words to twenty; the web of threads between every pair thickens disproportionately until it becomes a near-solid wall of light, and a counter drawn on the beam shows the pairs going 100 → 400 as the length doubles.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the read-in-order candle gutters at twenty rings while a translation lamp and a search box light; an honest card writes and crosses out three overclaims. CAMERA: the reverse flame push out to SHELF (low macro; the read-in-order candle goes out). Reverse flame push to the study shelf: the brightest knot of the wall of light from ch10-s12 becomes the flame of the read-in-order candle, and the camera pulls back out of that flame onto the shelf (never through black) while the light tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood serverCyan to candleAmber, no dip); the line waits until the amber is up. STUDY LOCK: the study is always candleAmber; the era enters only through practicals, here a dawnGold sky in the study window behind the shelf, the new day after the old belief. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Here LANGUAGE MUST BE READ IN ORDER (base tag 1997) has burned exactly twenty rings: a ghost sleeve twenty rings tall (120 px) stands above its stub. On 'decades' its flame gutters and goes out; the sleeve stays, dark, with a thread of smoke rising through the haze; the tag at its base now reads 1997–2017. On 'replaced' a soft cross-dissolve inside the smoke shows the new way spreading: a small lamp lit in a translation room and a search box lit in a window, each carrying a small in-world paper tag with its year, 2018 and 2019 (prop lettering, no caption) (the cross-dissolve's glow is warm dawn light through the window, never a re-tint of the study). Then, over the smoke, a parchment card writes the honest sentence one phrase at a time, wordless, starting just after L1030 ends, each phrase on its own beat: not the first attention; not only attention; built to translate. The card holds through the hold so all three can be read.
